The post Recursive Releases Flint, an Open-Weight 40B MoE Local Coding Model for Agents with 2.5B Active Params appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Recursive Superintelligence has released Flint , its first model. The Recursive Flint local coding model is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 40B total and 2.5B active parameters. Recursive team states that its Eureka Machine, an automated research system, helped build nearly every part of the stack. The weights are on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. TL;DR Size: 39.8B total, about 2.5B active per token. Context: 262,144 tokens documented on the model card; the blog cites up to 512k. Runs on: 48 GB Apple Silicon Macs (M4 Pro, M5 Pro, M5 Max) or 48 GB NVIDIA GPUs. 4-bit weights take about 23 GB. Performance: Tops Recursive’s chart among MoE models under 50B on agentic coding. Trails the strongest dense models. Best: IFEval 95.1%. SWE-bench Verified 74.2%. Worst: Terminal-Bench 2.1 at 54.9%, versus 73.0% for dense Qwen 3.8. What is Recursive Flint? Flint is a decoder-only MoE Transformer for coding agents. The model investigates codebases, fixes bugs, implements features and writes tests. It is text-only and supports reasoning and OpenAI-compatible tool calls. Introducing Flint, @Recursive_SI ’s first model: a fast local coding model built with our automated research system, the Eureka Machine. • Best-in-class fast local coding • Up to 2x faster than comparable models: 125+ tokens/sec on a MacBook Pro, 150+ on RTX Spark • Built from… pic.twitter.com/ufg2xScSGw — Richard Socher (@RichardSocher) October 21, 2026 How does Flint’s architecture work? Flint has 49 layers: 2 dense layers, then 47 MoE layers. Each MoE layer has 256 routed experts. A router selects 6 per token, plus 1 always-active shared expert. Attention mixes 2 types. 35 layers use a 513-token sliding window. 14 layers use full attention with no positional encoding. There are 32 query heads and 4 key/value heads. The 2.5B active figure includes the output head. The active body alone is about 2.2B parameters. How did the Eureka Machine build Flint? The Eureka Machine proposes ideas, implements them, tests them and picks what to try next. Recursive highlights 3 contributions: Architecture: It started from a 35B-total, 3B-active baseline. It searched expert configurations and widths, landing on 40B total and 2.5B active. Quantization: It quantized the output layer (lm_head) to 4 bits, against common practice. An offline distillation stage, with the 16-bit model as teacher, recovered accuracy. This nearly halved training steps versus a quantization-aware training baseline. The NVFP4 model scores within 0.7 points of the 16-bit model. Kernels: It wrote specialized kernels for low-bit projections, MoE operations, attention and prompt processing. On M4 and M5 chips, a Metal megakernel fuses the entire decode forward pass. How does Flint perform on coding benchmarks? All scores below are self-reported by Recursive. Sampling used temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95 and top-k 20. Benchmark Flint BF16 Flint NVFP4 Terminal-Bench 2.1 54.9% 53.7% SWE-bench Pro v2 89.7% 88.5% SWE-bench Verified 74.2% 74.1% LiveCodeBench v6 80.3% 80.8% IFBench 89.2% 88.1% IFEval 95.1% 94.6% Terminal-Bench used the Terminus 2 harness. Solutions found through web retrieval counted as failures. SWE-bench runs used mini-swe-agent with no internet access. Agentic scores average pass@1 over at least 5 attempts. In Recursive’s chart, Qwen3.6 scores 73.4% on SWE-bench Verified. Dense Qwen 3.8 scores 73.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, well above Flint. Recursive reports more than 125 tokens per second on an M4 Pro MacBook Pro. It reports more than 150 tokens per second on a 64 GB NVIDIA RTX Spark. Both are short-context figures, up to 2x faster than comparable models. It also claims Flint runs more than 5x faster than dense 25-40B models with similar coding scores. There are 3 local options: Apple Silicon: Flint INT4 MLX weights take about 22.6 GB. The rec engine needs an M4 Pro, M5 Pro or M5 Max with 48 GB memory. It reports 1.4 to 2.6x the throughput of llama.cpp on an M4 Pro. NVIDIA: The NVFP4 GGUF file is 22.9 GB. Recursive recommends at least 48 GB of GPU memory. Server: The 80 GB BF16 checkpoint needs 1 B300 or H200 GPU per replica. Flint also works with llama.cpp, Ollama, Unsloth, LM Studio, vLLM and SGLang. Key Takeaways Flint is a 40B MoE coding model with only 2.5B active parameters. It scores 74.2% on SWE-bench Verified and 54.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. 4-bit weights run in about 23 GB on a 48 GB Mac or GPU. It ranks #2 on the Open ASR Leaderboard with 5.68% average English WER, alongside updated Turbo CTC and 4.1 2B Plus models. The post IBM AI Releases Granite Speech 5.0 2B for Multilingual Transcription and Translation appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> IBM has released Granite Speech 5.0 2B , a new open speech-language model for transcription and translation. Granite Speech 5.0 2B is a 2B-parameter model from IBM that turns speech into text in 6 languages. It ships under Apache 2.0. IBM also updated 2 existing models : the edge-focused Turbo CTC and the diarization-focused 4.1 2B Plus. For developers, the release covers accurate transcription, fast on-device transcription and speaker-attributed transcripts. TL;DR Size: 2B parameters, dense. LLM backbone uses YaRN extension to 16k positions. IBM recommends audio segments of up to about 2 minutes. Runs on: GPU via Transformers or vLLM, Apple Silicon via mlx-audio, local CPU/Mac via llama.cpp GGUF (Q8_0 recommended). Performance: #2 open-weight model on the Open ASR Leaderboard, 5.68% average English WER. Best: 0.99% WER on LibriSpeech Clean. Worst: 13.79% WER on the leaderboard’s private conversational set. How does Granite Speech 5.0 2B work? The model has 3 parts, per the model card . A speech encoder of 16 Conformer blocks is trained with CTC. It uses block attention over 4-second audio blocks. A 2-layer window q-former then projects and downsamples the acoustic embeddings. Total downsampling is 10x, so the LLM sees embeddings at 10 Hz. The LLM is an intermediate checkpoint of granite-4.0-1b-base . IBM extended it to 16k positions with YaRN and fine-tuned it with LoRA adapters. Training used 390,000 hours of public audio plus synthetic data. The synthetic sets target Japanese ASR, keyword biasing and translation. Training took 40 days on 8 H100 GPUs. What is new versus Granite Speech 4.1 2B? Language ID prompting: name the input language in the prompt to steer transcription. Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: bias output toward product names, people and acronyms. Punctuation and capitalization on request: capitalization F1 runs from 90.16 to 99.51 across test sets. Robustness: better handling of noise, reverberation and distant microphones. How does Granite Speech 5.0 2B perform on benchmarks? On the Open ASR Leaderboard , IBM’s chart shows a 5.68% average English WER. That average covers 9 public and 2 private test sets, as of October 21, 2026. Only Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores better, at 5.40%. Note a source conflict. IBM’s blog reports 5.06% instead. That figure is unofficial, dated October 15, and averages public short-form sets only. Per-set results range widely. The model scores 0.99% on LibriSpeech Clean and 2.21% on LibriSpeech Other. It scores 13.79% on the private conversational set. On the noisy FFASR leaderboard , it ranks #4 of 42 at 14.80% average WER. Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores 13.41% there. Multilingual CommonVoice WER is 2.60% for Portuguese and 3.50% for Spanish. Japanese is the weakest language at 10.74%. For translation, X-to-English CoVoST BLEU reaches 53.6 for Portuguese and 40.1 for German. English-to-Mandarin was not evaluated. Keyword biasing shows the clearest gain. On Earnings-22, keyword F1 rises from 67.2 to 90.1 with correct keyword lists. With 2,000-term lists mixing correct and wrong terms, it still reaches 82.8. oldContent: We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs.rss We Work Remotely: Remote jobs in design, programming, marketing and more en-US 60 Apollo GraphQL: Senior Solution Engineer (Pre-sales) Anywhere in the World Georgia Sales and Marketing Full-Time <img src="https://we-work-remotely.imgix.net/logos/0171/6630/logo.gif?ixlib=rails-4.0.0&w=50&h=50&dpr=2&fit=fill&auto=compress" /> <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> San Francisco, California, United States <br /><strong>URL:</strong> <a href="https://apollographql.com">https://apollographql.com</a> </p> <p>At Apollo GraphQL, we’re on a mission to make it radically easier for engineering teams to ship fast, reliable products and services on top of the world’s data, powering everything from web to mobile to agentic experiences..</p> <p>We’re looking for a Senior Solution Engineer who loves stepping into business‑critical challenges and turning them into clear, elegant architectures that customers can’t wait to build. As a Senior SE, you’ll be the technical quarterback on some of our most important opportunities: partnering with prospects and customers to design and scale their supergraph on GraphOS, and helping them prove out real impact in production.</p> <p>You’ll join a tight‑knit global SE team that collaborates closely with Sales, Marketing, Product, and Engineering—so the work you do doesn’t just close deals, it directly shapes Apollo’s roadmap and how we show up in the market.</p> <p>At its core, this role connects customer problems, Apollo’s capabilities, and value: uncovering the real problem, translating technical options into business outcomes, building technical confidence, and reducing buying risk.</p> <h2>What you’ll do</h2> <ul> <li> <p><strong>Own complex technical evaluations</strong> for strategic new and existing accounts: lead discovery, workshops, and solution design to deeply understand customer APIs, architectures, and constraints, and turn them into clear required capabilities and technical win plans.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Design and present multi‑system solution architectures</strong> that show how Apollo’s supergraph, GraphOS, and tooling fit into modern cloud‑native environments —meeting customers where they are while charting a safe, future‑proof path forward.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Lead compelling, value‑focused demos and PoCs</strong>, translating complex technical capabilities into simple, business‑aligned stories for audiences ranging from lead developers and architects to VP/C‑suite decision makers.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>De‑risk and win complex deals</strong> by anticipating and resolving technical blockers (security, compliance, integration, performance), building customer confidence that Apollo will work in their environment, and partnering with AEs on value‑based selling, and close strategy.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Partner tightly with Sales, CS, Product, and Engineering</strong>: act as a trusted advisor throughout the account lifecycle, feed structured field insight back into roadmap and positioning, and contribute reusable reference architectures, playbooks, and patterns that the broader team can use at scale.</p> </li> <li> <p><strong>Elevate the team through enablement and AI‑augmented workflows</strong>: mentor junior SEs, share best practices, and actively use AI tooling oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Tue, 20 Oct 2026 16:10:34 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.11 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 When A Startup Sells, Its Employees’ Equity Plans Can Change Overnight https://news.crunchbase.com/ma/acquired-startup-employees-equity-plans-from-honig/ Wed, 21 Oct 2026 11:00:38 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94255 By Ron Honig Acquisitions are reshaping the technology industry. Venture-backed AI companies acquired 195 AI startups this year through late September , already exceeding the total for all of 2025, Crunchbase data shows. For investors and founders, such acquisitions can represent major financial milestones. For employees holding equity compensation, a transaction can also change personal financial plans they had expected to follow for years. A client whose employer was acquired in an all-cash transaction described to me the atmosphere inside the company during the weeks that followed: Employees repeatedly discussed the deal in office corridors, trying to understand what it meant for their equity awards, their jobs and their future. She compared the confusion to the atmosphere surrounding a major reorganization or a round of layoffs. The transaction offered the prospect of substantial financial gains. Yet employees were struggling to establish what those gains would mean for them individually. One acquisition, different outcomes Ron Honig, co-CEO of From-Honig Family Office. Employees at the same company can emerge from an acquisition with remarkably different financial outcomes. Some own vested shares. Others hold restricted stock units, stock options or performance-based awards. Their rights depend on grant agreements, vesting conditions and transaction terms. Even two employees holding RSUs may face different payment schedules or employment requirements. Depending on the agreements, outstanding awards may be settled in cash, accelerated, converted into replacement awards, or remain subject to future conditions. One employee might receive a substantial payment when the transaction closes. Another may have much of the expected value tied to continued employment. The announced acquisition price provides a reference point. It rarely tells an individual employee everything they need to know about the money they will receive. This helps explain the conversations my client described. Colleagues may compare the value of their equity without realizing that their contractual rights differ. Wealth and employment uncertainty Technology employees with substantial equity compensation often depend on their employer in several ways. Their salaries, bonuses, career opportunities and investment portfolios may all be linked to the same company. An all-cash acquisition can reduce their exposure to its share price once vested shares are converted into cash. Other forms of dependence may continue. The acquiring company may reorganize teams, change responsibilities or introduce retention arrangements. Employees whose unvested awards remain conditional on employment may face difficult choices about staying. Someone expecting a large payment can therefore feel financially stronger while becoming less certain about their career. Before making plans A major acquisition announcement can change personal ambitions long before the proceeds arrive. Employees may begin considering early retirement, a new business, a career break or a major family purchase. Those possibilities are worth exploring. But an announced acquisition may still require regulatory approvals and other closing conditions. The headline value of an equity award may differ substantially from the cash ultimately available to its holder. Taxes, exercise costs where applicable, outstanding liabilities and payment schedules can all affect the outcome. So can the employee’s financial position outside the company. A substantial payment might make a career change affordable without providing enough capital to fund permanent retirement. Existing pension savings, household spending and future earning capacity remain important. In my work with technology executives, I have seen expectations about new wealth reshape personal plans before the underlying numbers have been established. Employees facing a cash acquisition can begin with three questions: What rights do my specific awards provide? When will the proceeds actually become available? And what choices will the resulting after-tax capital support? The answers may differ considerably among colleagues. An exit without an exit decision Founders who sell their companies often participate directly in negotiating the transaction. Employees holding equity compensation generally have much less influence over its timing. They may have intended to retain their shares for years, sell gradually or remain employed until additional awards vested. A corporate acquisition can replace those plans with a timetable established by the transaction. For some employees, the result will be substantial financial flexibility. For others, a significant part of their expected compensation may remain connected to future employment. The period between announcement and closing can be especially difficult because the financial opportunity is visible while important details remain unresolved. My client’s description of the office corridors captured that experience. The company had made a decision about its future. Its employees were left to work out what that decision meant for theirs. The acquisition determines the terms of a corporate transaction. Each employee still has to establish how much financial freedom it creates. Ron Honig is co-CEO and managing partner of From-Honig Family Office , which works with technology executives, founders and families on integrated wealth planning, equity compensation and major liquidity events. His background includes more than two decades in the technology industry. Disclosure: The views expressed are the author’s own. This article is for general informational purposes and does not constitute financial, investment, legal or tax advice. Details of the client experience have been presented without identifying information. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Thu, 22 Oct 2026 14:12:42 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.11 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Exclusive: Slingshot Raises $27M In Seed Funding To Build An Insurer For Those Small Policies Sold At Checkout https://news.crunchbase.com/fintech-ecommerce/insuretech/startup-slingshot-insurance-seed-funding-genteman/ Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:00:23 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94267 Slingshot Insurance , an AI-native embedded insurance startup, is emerging from stealth with $27 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. Rally Ventures and Skyward Group co-led the round, with participation from insurance industry veterans including Jim Hays , who will join Slingshot’s board. Rally is also a co-founder of the Minneapolis-based startup, as part of the firm’s broader approach. So far, it has co-founded roughly eight portfolio companies that have either launched or remain in stealth. Ethan Genteman, co-founder and CEO of Slingshot Insurance. (Courtesy photo) Slingshot, which is led by first-time founder and CEO Ethan Genteman , focuses on small insurance policies that consumers can buy as part of another purchase, such as coverage when booking a flight. Known as embedded insurance, the model puts coverage in front of customers when they might need it. The startup’s software helps businesses offer those policies by connecting them with insurers that back the coverage. It uses AI to process and share data between the two sides, aiming to reduce the administrative work that can make inexpensive policies costly to offer. Its first customer and design partner is Vertical Insure , which serves more than 750,000 customers at an average premium of $25, according to Slingshot. Genteman told Crunchbase News that Slingshot’s first program will launch this month. For now, Slingshot earns revenue as a technology provider working with outside insurers. But the six-person company, which formally began operating July 1, is also pursuing an acquisition that would allow it to back policies itself. “We’re not a carrier yet, but we are rapidly closing on our carrier,” Genteman said in an interview. Making the math work on a $25 policy One product Slingshot is working on would let parents buy insurance when signing a child up for youth sports, Genteman said. A parent spending $2,000 on a volleyball league, for example, might be offered a $25 policy covering cancellation or an injury during the season. Each policy includes paperwork and coordination with an insurer, and can bring potential claims. But when policies cost so little, managing them can quickly eat into the money they bring in, noted Genteman. He believes that as vertical SaaS companies increasingly look beyond traditional subscription fees for growth, embedded insurance is “a largely untapped opportunity” to generate incremental revenue from transactions already happening on their platforms while delivering additional value to customers. “The challenge is that the insurance and regulatory landscape is incredibly complex, and most SaaS companies don’t have the expertise, industry relationships or understanding of where to begin,” he said. Slingshot aims to solve this by providing a white-glove service for those vertical SaaS companies, helping them go from an insurance product idea to “a fully operational offering.” He offered a hypothetical example: A program collecting $500,000 in premiums with a 10% margin would have just $50,000 in margin. “That’s not a viable program for the way incumbent carriers have set themselves up operationally,” he said. Slingshot’s goal is to replace the spreadsheets, emails and disconnected systems used to manage that work with software that connects policy distributors and insurers directly. The company says its AI automates data-heavy tasks while keeping a record of decisions that the businesses involved can review and check. It charges a 5% technology fee to administer programs through its platform. Acquiring an insurer would let it provide both the software and the financial backing, according to Genteman. A customer helped shape the business The difficulties facing Slingshot’s first customer helped bring the startup together. Rally had already helped start Vertical Insure, which uses software platforms to sell insurance to its customers. According to Genteman, that business had opportunities to introduce more products but struggled to find insurers whose technology and processes could keep up. “We can design the products our customers need almost overnight, but the industry is highly regulated, and we need delegated authority just to write and distribute what we’ve built,” Vertical Insure co-founder and CEO Brock Noland said in a statement. “The antiquated approval process on the carrier-side slows everything down.” Even after finding an insurer willing to back a product, connecting the two companies’ systems could create more delays, Genteman said. Slingshot was built to address those problems, with Vertical Insure helping shape its product as a design partner. Noland is also a Slingshot co-founder. The opportunity in vertical SaaS Genteman sees a broader opening among vertical SaaS companies: businesses that sell software tailored to a particular industry. As vertical SaaS companies look for ways to grow beyond subscription fees, insurance could give them another avenue to make money from purchases customers already make through their platforms, argues Genteman. They already know their customers and what they’re buying, putting them in a position to offer coverage that fits the purchase. A babysitting platform, for example, could offer coverage to help parents pay for replacement childcare if a sitter cancels at the last minute. Software used by pet boarding facilities could offer coverage for unexpected vet bills if a pet is injured during a stay. An equipment rental platform could let customers add protection at checkout against accidental damage or theft. Those are examples of what could be developed, Genteman said. Before joining Rally, he ran SportsEngine , where insurance sold through its software became a key revenue source. “That experience gave me firsthand insight into the opportunity for software companies to generate revenue through embedded financial products,” he wrote via email. Kaufenberg sees similar potential across Rally’s portfolio, where most companies combine AI products with financial services. He said founders increasingly want insurance partners that can help them introduce coverage quickly. The post IBM AI Releases Granite Speech 5.0 2B for Multilingual Transcription and Translation appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> IBM has released Granite Speech 5.0 2B , a new open speech-language model for transcription and translation. Granite Speech 5.0 2B is a 2B-parameter model from IBM that turns speech into text in 6 languages. It ships under Apache 2.0. IBM also updated 2 existing models : the edge-focused Turbo CTC and the diarization-focused 4.1 2B Plus. For developers, the release covers accurate transcription, fast on-device transcription and speaker-attributed transcripts. TL;DR Size: 2B parameters, dense. LLM backbone uses YaRN extension to 16k positions. IBM recommends audio segments of up to about 2 minutes. Runs on: GPU via Transformers or vLLM, Apple Silicon via mlx-audio, local CPU/Mac via llama.cpp GGUF (Q8_0 recommended). Performance: #2 open-weight model on the Open ASR Leaderboard, 5.68% average English WER. Best: 0.99% WER on LibriSpeech Clean. Worst: 13.79% WER on the leaderboard’s private conversational set. How does Granite Speech 5.0 2B work? The model has 3 parts, per the model card . A speech encoder of 16 Conformer blocks is trained with CTC. It uses block attention over 4-second audio blocks. A 2-layer window q-former then projects and downsamples the acoustic embeddings. Total downsampling is 10x, so the LLM sees embeddings at 10 Hz. The LLM is an intermediate checkpoint of granite-4.0-1b-base . IBM extended it to 16k positions with YaRN and fine-tuned it with LoRA adapters. Training used 390,000 hours of public audio plus synthetic data. The synthetic sets target Japanese ASR, keyword biasing and translation. Training took 40 days on 8 H100 GPUs. What is new versus Granite Speech 4.1 2B? Language ID prompting: name the input language in the prompt to steer transcription. Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: bias output toward product names, people and acronyms. Punctuation and capitalization on request: capitalization F1 runs from 90.16 to 99.51 across test sets. Robustness: better handling of noise, reverberation and distant microphones. How does Granite Speech 5.0 2B perform on benchmarks? On the Open ASR Leaderboard , IBM’s chart shows a 5.68% average English WER. That average covers 9 public and 2 private test sets, as of October 21, 2026. Only Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores better, at 5.40%. Note a source conflict. IBM’s blog reports 5.06% instead. That figure is unofficial, dated October 15, and averages public short-form sets only. Per-set results range widely. The model scores 0.99% on LibriSpeech Clean and 2.21% on LibriSpeech Other. It scores 13.79% on the private conversational set. On the noisy FFASR leaderboard , it ranks #4 of 42 at 14.80% average WER. Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores 13.41% there. Multilingual CommonVoice WER is 2.60% for Portuguese and 3.50% for Spanish. Japanese is the weakest language at 10.74%. For translation, X-to-English CoVoST BLEU reaches 53.6 for Portuguese and 40.1 for German. English-to-Mandarin was not evaluated. Keyword biasing shows the clearest gain. On Earnings-22, keyword F1 rises from 67.2 to 90.1 with correct keyword lists. With 2,000-term lists mixing correct and wrong terms, it still reaches 82.8. How does it compare with other open ASR models? Feature Granite Speech 5.0 2B Qwen3-ASR-1.7B Cohere Transcribe 03-2026 Canary-Qwen-2.5B Size 2B 2.35B (Hub count) 2.07B (Hub count) 2.5B License Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 (gated) CC-BY-4.0 ASR languages 6 30 + 22 Chinese dialects 14 English only Speech translation Yes Not disclosed Not disclosed No Open ASR avg WER (Oct 21, 2026)* 5.68% 5.40% 5.77% 5.94% FFASR avg WER (Oct 18, 2026)* 14.80% 13.41% 15.03% Not disclosed Keyword biasing Up to 2,000 terms Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Long audio ~2 min segments Long audio supported Not disclosed 40 s max in training *Leaderboard averages as charted in IBM’s model card from the Open ASR and FFASR leaderboards. What changed in Turbo CTC and 4.1 2B Plus? Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC keeps its 470M footprint. It now transcribes 7 languages with native punctuation and capitalization. IBM compiled one Conformer block and reused its graph across the stack. That lifted throughput to 19,870 RTFx, up from about 12,600 at launch. The updated Granite Speech 4.1 2B Plus is a drop-in weight update. Average timestamp shift falls from 210.86 to 98.54. Long-form WER drops from 13.53 to 10.22. Biased-keyword WER falls from 11.79 to 6.48. How can developers deploy it? Granite Speech 5.0 2B runs in Transformers , vLLM, llama.cpp and mlx-audio. For GGUF, IBM recommends Q8_0. Lower-bit quantizations lose accuracy on audio longer than about 1 minute. Key Takeaways #2 open-weight model on the Open ASR Leaderboard at 5.68% WER. 2B parameters, Apache 2.0, runs on GPU, Mac and local CPU. 2,000-term keyword biasing across all supported languages. Turbo CTC reaches 19,870 RTFx and now covers 7 languages. Qwen3-ASR-1.7B still leads on accuracy and noisy audio. Check out the model card , IBM blog and Granite Speech paper . The post Liquid AI Launches RIPL, a Real-Time Inference Engine for Sub-50 ms LFMs appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Liquid AI just announced Liquid RIPL , short for Real-time Inference Pipeline. RIPL is a low-latency engine that serves Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) inside a live request path. It returns complete generated responses end-to-end in under 50 ms. It also claims that latency holds while traffic arrives continuously at peak load. For developers, the message is simple. Swap gradient-boosted trees for a generative model, and keep the latency budget. TL;DR Engine : Serves LFM2.5 models from 230M to 2.6B parameters Runs on: Enterprise deployments on NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs. Benchmarks used a single B200. Performance: 5.6 to 28.4x lower p95 latency than Qwen3.5 on vLLM, per Liquid’s own tests. Best: LFM2.5-1.2B hit 155.8 ms p95 vs 4,431 ms for Qwen3.5-0.8B, a 28.4x gap (256 in, 128 out). Worst: LFM2.5-2.6B gained only 5.6x (449.1 ms vs 2,499 ms). Sub-50 ms fails on longer requests. What problem does Liquid RIPL solve? Most serving stacks target large batches and long agentic jobs. A few seconds per request is acceptable there. Search ranking, fraud checks and payment authorization need answers in milliseconds. Liquid AI argues teams default to classical models for these paths because LLM serving is too slow. RIPL is built to remove that trade-off. How does RIPL work? Liquid AI describes RIPL as optimizing the full path, from request arrival to completed response. In several workloads, Liquid AI plots the same model, LFM2.5-350M, on vLLM and on RIPL. RIPL’s p95 line sits well below the vLLM line in each case. That isolates part of the gain to the engine, not just the model architecture. The LFM2.5 models themselves are hybrids. LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct has 16 layers: 10 double-gated convolution blocks and 6 GQA blocks. LFM2.5-2.6B has 30 layers: 22 convolution blocks and 8 GQA blocks. RIPL benchmarks: how fast is it vs vLLM? Liquid measured p95 end-to-end latency under open-loop Poisson arrivals on one B200. LFMs ran on RIPL. Baselines, including MiniCPM5 and Granite 4.2, ran on vLLM. Performance: top English Elo among open models Gradium tested; about 7 ms to first audio on CPU. Best: 1.70% WER on a 500-sentence hard set, versus 3.50% for Kokoro (Gradium’s eval). Worst: 0.51% Seed-TTS LLM WER, behind Kokoro (0.45%) and Magpie (0.46%). What is Gradium Phonon? Phonon is an open-weight TTS family from Gradium , a Paris voice AI company spun out of Kyutai. It generates speech locally on phones, laptops, boards and browsers. The family has three models : Phonon 31m: English only, 37 built-in voices, Apache 2.0. Phonon 40m: 1 model per language (English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese), CC BY-NC 4.0. Phonon 40m multilingual: all 5 languages in 1 model, 102 voices, CC BY-NC 4.0. How does Phonon work? Phonon uses a causal transformer backbone. Its prefix combines text and speaker embeddings. A SentencePiece tokenizer with a 4,000-token vocabulary reads raw text, with no phoneme conversion. The backbone generates 1 latent vector per 80 ms frame. A flow-matching head turns that vector plus noise into an audio embedding in a single step. A smaller variant of Kyutai’s Mimi decoder then outputs 24 kHz PCM audio. A separate end-of-speech head decides when to stop. Phonon 31m uses 6 transformer layers, width 512 and 8 attention heads. Our mobile-first app gives more than 2 million users access to the latest tokens, tokenized stocks, and leverage trading, with over $4B in volume processed since launch in 2024. Every trade, auto-sell, and fee flow runs on-chain, and the contracts behind them have to be fast, safe, and correct.</p> <p><strong>The Role</strong><br>You’ll own the on-chain programs that power Moonshot’s trading products on Solana and EVM chains. You’ll take each contract from spec through audit to production, and help design how we expand to new chains and products. We’re a small team, so you’ll join early and ship real code fast. Expect your first production deployment within your first two weeks.</p> <p><strong>What You’ll Do</strong></p> <p>Own core trading programs, including order execution, auto-sell, fee routing, and token launch, from specification to deployment and audit<br>Design cross-chain and settlement paths alongside our protocol engineers<br>Build and maintain a thorough test suite using Anchor tests, Foundry, and property-based fuzzing<br>Work directly with our security auditors on each release cycle</p> <p><strong>You Might Be a Fit If You</strong></p> <p>Have shipped production programs on Solana (Anchor) or an EVM L2, ideally securing more than $10M in TVL or volume<br>Can debug at the bytecode level when something breaks at 2 a.m.<br>Value the unglamorous work: testing, fuzzing, formal verification, and audits<br>Have delivered at least one end-to-end cross-chain integration (bridges, oracles, or settlement)<br>Understand trading mechanics such as slippage, MEV, and transaction ordering on Solana</p> <p><strong>Compensation &amp; Benefits</strong></p> <p>$150K base salary plus meaningful early-stage equity<br>Full health, dental, and vision coverage (US-based hires)<br>$2,000 annual learning budget</p> <p><strong>To apply:</strong> <a href="https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/moonshot-solidity-rust-remote">https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/moonshot-solidity-rust-remote</a></p> Thu, 22 Oct 2026 13:00:33 +0000 Sat, 21 Nov 2026 13:00:33 +0000 https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/moonshot-solidity-rust-remote https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/moonshot-solidity-rust-remote Affirm: Analytics Engineer II, Full Stack (Revenue Analytics) Anywhere in the World Full-Stack Programming Full-Time <p> <strong>Headquarters:</strong> Remote Poland </p> <div class="content-intro"><p>At Affirm, we exist for the moments that matter—giving people a clear, predictable way to pay over time, with no hidden fees, no surprises, and no tradeoffs on what matters most.</p></div><p>We’re looking for a curious, driven professional to join our Revenue Analytics team. This builds and owns the data products, reporting infrastructure, semantic foundations, and analytical systems that power Affirm’s Revenue organization.<br>As a Senior Analyst, Revenue Analytics, you’ll build scalable data products that power day-to-day decision-making - owning end-to-end work across data modeling, metric definitions, dashboards, automation, and enablement.&nbsp;<br>You’ll also help strengthen our semantic layer and data governance, laying the foundation for reliable AI. The ideal candidate combines strong technical and analytical skills with the ability to turn ambiguous business questions into durable, well-tested data infrastructure.</p> <p><strong>What you'll do</strong>&nbsp;</p> <ul> <li> <p>Develop dbt data models, dashboards, metrics, and automation processes for the revenue field team and revenue analysts</p> </li> <li> <p>Build and maintain critical reporting data models that power external merchant reporting&nbsp;</p> </li> <li> <p>Build the semantic, metadata, and context layers that allow AI systems to accurately understand Revenue data, metrics, and business definitions</p> </li> <li> <p>Partner with Business Systems, engineering, and business stakeholders to translate requirements into durable, well-tested data products</p> </li> <li> <p>Contribute to the team’s best practices in version control, code review, documentation, and release hygiene (GitHub-based workflows)</p> </li> <li> <p>Develop processes, governance, and foundations to scale the impact of analytics within Revenue.</p> </li> </ul> <p><br><strong>What we look for</strong>&nbsp;</p> <ul> <li> <p>3+ years of work experience in an analytics engineering or business intelligence role</p> </li> <li> <p>Strong working knowledge of SQL, dbt, Python, data modeling, and data visualization&nbsp;</p> </li> <li> <p>Hands-on experience with BI tools (Sigma/Looker/Tableau), Databricks, and cloud data warehouses (Snowflake)</p> </li> <li> <p>Understanding of the data foundations required for reliable AI, including semantic layers, metadata, evals, metric definitions, documentation, and data quality</p> </li> <li> <p>Demonstrated experience integrating AI tools into day-to-day analytics engineering workflows to improve development speed,
